title: The mobile visit for a community sports club

excerpt: Most people will judge a club on a phone. The first screen still has to show people playing, how to start, and membership or the schedule.

faqs.question: What has to fit on the first phone screen?
faqs.answer: A recognizable picture of play, a sentence on how to start, and a tappable path to membership or the schedule. If the link sits below the first view, the phone page is a poster. Design that screen before you fall in love with the wide layout.

faqs.question: How should a timetable work on a phone?
faqs.answer: Rebuild a noticeboard grid as a list grouped by day, with the session, the time, the place, and who it is for. Put the entrance note in the same view as the time. A person in the car park needs tonight, not a matrix they have to pinch.

faqs.question: What loading targets matter on a club phone page?
faqs.answer: The Web Vitals guidance calls for Largest Contentful Paint within two and a half seconds, Interaction to Next Paint at 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift at or below one tenth, judged at the 75th percentile of loads. On a club phone page that means a lead photo sized for the device, and a schedule link that does not jump under the thumb.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A community sports club mobile website is the visit most people will use when they decide whether to join. The first screen still has to show people playing, how to start, and a way to see membership or the schedule. Design that screen at the width of the phone. A desktop composition can be a later luxury.

The phone visit is often outdoors, one-handed, with poor signal, between a message from a friend and the decision to leave the house. The page has to survive that visit.

## The first screen, at thumb width

Open the design on a phone before you discuss the wide hero. The picture of play should be recognizable without pinching. The sentence on how to start should be readable without zooming. The link to membership or the schedule should be on that first view, with a target a thumb can hit. If any of those three slip below the first view, the phone page is a poster.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) gives you about 10 seconds to show value before many visitors leave. On a phone the screen holds less, so those seconds contain fewer elements. Spend them on the activity, the start, and the door. A logo animation, a cookie wall, and a slogan consume the same seconds and answer nothing.

Type size is part of the content. A clever condensed face that looked sharp on a studio monitor will fail in daylight on a pitch-side path. Use a size and a weight a stranger can read at arm's length. Contrast belongs to the same decision. Pale gray on a photograph is a desktop affectation. Put the words on a solid ground if the picture is busy.

The button label stays in the club's words. Schedule. Membership. Trial. The same words as the header. A phone has no patience for a synonym.

## What the desktop layout tries to steal

Wide layouts like a cinematic crop, a side-by-side column of prose, and a menu that only fits when the window is large. Those choices smuggle themselves onto the phone as a tiny crop, a wall of text, and a hidden drawer. Review the phone as its own page. Ask what the wide layout was allowed to add, not what the phone must shrink.

A common theft is the horizontal card row. On a desktop it shows four sessions. On a phone it becomes a swipe the visitor never discovers, so they see one session and think it is the only session. Stack the sessions, or show two with a clear control. The schedule is too important to hide in a gesture.

Another theft is the video header. It autoplays, eats the connection, and shows six seconds of atmosphere before the door. If you keep a video, keep it muted, secondary, and skippable, and put the still image and the link first. People on a train should get the decision even when the video never loads.

Pop-ups that ask for an email address before the schedule appears are a third theft. The member's errand was the schedule. Collect an address after they have seen the thing they came for, if you collect one at all. A club that answers by email can publish the address. It does not need to ransom the timetable.

## Speed, stability, and the thumb

A phone on a club's wifi, or on a weak signal in a sports ground, will expose a heavy page. Core Web Vitals, as [web.dev describes them](https://web.dev/articles/vitals), cover three parts of that experience. Largest Contentful Paint should occur within 2.5 seconds for a good loading experience. Interaction to Next Paint should be 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift should stay at 0.1 or less. The recommended way to judge this is the 75th percentile of page loads, on mobile and on desktop.

Translate that into club decisions. The lead photograph should be a real file size, cropped for the phone, not a print-resolution image scaled down by the browser. The button should not jump downward when a font or a banner arrives late. The menu should respond the moment it is tapped. A layout shift that moves the Schedule link under a thumb at the wrong instant is how a person calls the wrong number or opens the wrong page.

You do not need a performance lab to do the first check. Load the page on a phone, on a normal connection, and watch what arrives first. If the first thing is a slider of sponsors, the priority is wrong. If the picture of play and the link arrive together and stay still, you are close.

Hanabi builds marketing sites in Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, hosted with the rest of the studio's stack on Vercel. The reason to mention the stack here is practical. A phone page stays fast when the first screen is simple and the images are deliberate. Clever effects are optional. The schedule link is not.

## The schedule itself, on a small screen

The timetable is the page most likely to break. A grid designed for a noticeboard becomes a horizontal smear on a phone. Rebuild it as a list grouped by day, with the session name, the time, the place, and who it is for. Let the reader jump to Today or to Juniors. A person in the car park needs tonight, not a matrix.

Put the address and a map link on the same view as the time. "Hall B, side entrance" can be the difference between a good first visit and a wrong door. Long driving directions can fold open. The first line should be enough to start walking.

Membership on a phone should show the price shape without a download. If a PDF is unavoidable for the committee archive, the HTML still has to carry the number, the period, and what is included. Pinch-zooming a scanned flyer is how you lose the person you almost convinced.

Forms should use the right keyboards: email, telephone, number. Error messages should say what to fix, next to the field. A parent typing with one hand will abandon a form that clears itself. Save nothing magical. Just do not punish a small typo with a blank page.

## Touch, motion, and glare

Buttons and links need space around them so a thumb does not open Sponsors while reaching for Fees. The W3C accessibility guidelines matter here in spirit even when you are mainly thinking about rain and cold hands. Operable means the control can be used. On a phone that means size, contrast, and a name.

If anything moves, it should earn the motion. A schedule that animates in, row by row, delays the fact. Respect the system setting for reduced motion. People who set it include members with vestibular disorders and members who simply hate a menu that bounces. Both deserve the still version.

Glare is a design condition. Outdoors, a pale low-contrast page disappears. Dark text on a light solid background, and a button that looks like a button, will survive sunshine better than a translucent bar over a photograph. Test the homepage in daylight once. It takes five minutes and it will change your mind about gray.

Try the page in the actual conditions of a first visit. Stand outside the hall, on the club's own connection if it has one, and open the homepage. Can you name the sport. Can you find tonight. Can you tap the fee without zooming. If the answer fails, the desktop file you admired in a meeting is not the site your members have. Fix the phone and let the wide layout inherit the same order: picture of play, how to start, membership or the schedule.

Shared phones matter in junior clubs. A parent may hand the screen to another parent in the car park. The page should still make sense if the visitor has never seen your desktop version and never will. Avoid instructions that say "hover" or "see the menu on the left." There is no left menu on the device in their hand. Write the interface for the device that showed up.

Write times in the club's local form and keep the day name next to the hour. A list that says only 19:00 forces a translation the visitor is doing in a doorway. Thursday, 7 p.m., Hall B is a sentence they can act on. If two sessions share a start time in different places, the place has to be in the same line as the time. A footnote is where wrong turns are born.

## From the phone to the person who still needs a human

Some visits should end in a conversation: a junior whose age sits on the boundary, a player coming back from injury, a question the schedule cannot answer. The contact path has to say what happens next, how soon, and what to have ready. It should stay shorter than a club application. That path is [a contact path for a community sports club](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-community-sports-club).

If you want to look at the phone version of a site with someone who builds them, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Open your current site on your phone before the call, and note the first thing you see.
